With a parameterized query, the driver or database treats the value strictly as data, whatever characters it contains. This is the primary defence. Manual escaping and blocklists of words such as `DROP` are unreliable and should not be used in its place.

Parameters do not cover every part of a query:

| Query part                | Safe approach                                             |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Values                    | Bound parameters                                          |
| Column or table names     | Map user input to a hardcoded allowlist                   |
| Sort direction            | Allow only `ASC` or `DESC`                                |
| `IN (...)` lists          | Generate one placeholder per value, or bind an array      |
| Raw queries in an [ORM](node:ORM) | Use the ORM's parameter binding, never interpolation |
| Dynamic SQL in stored procedures | Bind parameters there too                          |

An ORM protects its normal query methods, but its raw-query features can still be injected. Stored data can also be dangerous: in second-order injection, a value saved safely is later concatenated into another query, so treat values read from your own database as untrusted too.

Add defence in depth. Connect with a database account holding the least privileges it needs, so that an injection cannot drop tables. Return generic error messages, since raw database errors help attackers refine a payload. Input validation is useful but does not replace parameters.
quotes: Search crashes whenever the term contains an apostrophe.
That's SQL injection waiting to happen. Replace the string formatting with a bound parameter.

nodes.name: SSRF
nodes.description: An attack that tricks your server into requesting a URL of the attacker's choice, often reaching internal systems.
nodes.markdown:
SSRF (server-side request forgery) is a vulnerability where an attacker makes your server send a request to a destination they choose. It appears in features that fetch a user-supplied URL: link previews, image imports, PDF generators and [webhook](node:Webhook) destinations. The request originates inside your network, so it can reach things the attacker cannot reach directly, including admin panels, internal APIs and cloud metadata endpoints.

Many cloud platforms expose instance information at the link-local address `169.254.169.254`, sometimes including temporary credentials. If an "import image from URL" feature fetches that address and returns the body, the attacker may obtain those credentials.

Blocklisting strings such as `localhost` is not sufficient. Attackers can use alternate IP encodings, IPv6 forms, a DNS name resolving to an internal address, or a public URL that redirects inward. Apply layered controls:

| Control                  | What to do                                                                |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Allowlist                | Permit only known hosts wherever the feature allows it                    |
| Scheme and port          | Allow only `https`, or `http` if required, on expected ports              |
| Resolved IP check        | Resolve the name and reject private, loopback, link-local and mapped addresses |
| Pin the connection       | Connect to the validated IP, which prevents DNS rebinding                 |
| Redirects                | Disable them, or revalidate every hop                                     |
| Network egress           | Run fetchers in an isolated network with outbound rules                   |
| Metadata hardening       | Require session-based metadata access, such as AWS IMDSv2                 |
| Response handling        | Enforce size and time limits, and do not return raw bodies or errors      |

DNS rebinding is why checking a URL once is not enough: the name resolves to a public address during validation and an internal one at fetch time.

Return one generic failure, since differing errors let attackers map internal ports. Internal services should still require [authentication](node:Authentication) instead of trusting a request because it came from inside.
quotes: The link preview fetched `169.254.169.254` during the pen test.
That's SSRF. Validate the resolved IP, pin the connection and block redirects.

nodes.name: Concurrency
nodes.description: Structuring a program so several tasks are in progress over the same period, whether or not they run at the same instant.
nodes.markdown:
Concurrency is structuring a program so that several tasks are in progress during the same period. The tasks may take turns on a single CPU core, which distinguishes it from [parallelism](node:Parallelism), where tasks execute at the same instant. A server needs concurrency because requests overlap: while one waits for a database response, another can use the CPU.

Languages and runtimes offer different models:

| Model                                  | Who switches tasks                  | Examples                          |
| -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| OS [threads](node:Thread)              | Operating system, at any moment     | Java platform threads, C++        |
| Runtime-managed threads                | Language runtime                    | Goroutines, Java virtual threads  |
| [Event loop](node:Event%20loop) tasks  | Tasks yield at [await](node:Async-await) points | Node.js, Python asyncio |
| Multiple processes                     | Operating system, memory isolated   | Pre-fork web servers              |

Concurrency helps most when work spends its time waiting, such as on network calls, disk access or a database. It does little for a task that uses the CPU continuously, because there is no idle time for another task to use.

The difficulty comes from shared state. When tasks overlap, their steps can interleave in orders you did not plan for. That produces the typical concurrency bug: code passes every test with one user, then under load a counter comes up short or two customers book the same seat. Such a [race condition](node:Race%20condition) may appear only rarely, which makes it hard to reproduce.

Protecting shared data with a [mutex](node:Mutex) solves that but adds waiting, and careless locking can produce a [deadlock](node:Deadlock). Where possible, avoid sharing mutable state, or let the database enforce the rule atomically.

Limit concurrency as well. Launching one task per item in a list of 100,000 can exhaust connections, memory or a partner's rate limit. A [thread pool](node:Thread%20pool) or semaphore (a counter capping simultaneous tasks) keeps the number bounded.
quotes: It works perfectly when I test it, but production totals are a few cents off.
That sounds like a concurrency bug. Two requests are probably updating the same balance at once.

nodes.name: Parallelism
nodes.description: Executing multiple computations at the same instant on separate CPU cores to finish CPU-heavy work sooner.
nodes.markdown:
Parallelism is executing multiple computations at the same instant on separate CPU cores. It is often confused with [concurrency](node:Concurrency), which is about managing overlapping tasks. A single-core machine can be concurrent by switching between tasks, but it cannot be parallel.

| Situation                         | Concurrent | Parallel | What helps                     |
| --------------------------------- | ---------- | -------- | ------------------------------ |
| 1,000 requests waiting on network | Yes        | Not needed | [Async-await](node:Async-await) or many [threads](node:Thread) |
| Resizing images on 8 cores        | Possibly   | Yes      | One task per core              |
| One long sequential calculation   | No         | No       | A faster algorithm             |

Parallelism speeds up CPU-bound work, meaning work limited by computation rather than waiting. Adding cores to an I/O-bound service often changes little, because its time is spent waiting on something else.

Speedup has a limit. Amdahl's law states that the serial portion of a program caps the benefit of adding processors. If 10% of a job must run sequentially, it can never go more than ten times faster, however many cores you add. Coordination, such as waiting on a [mutex](node:Mutex), adds further cost, and past some point more threads can make a program slower.

Runtimes differ in what they allow. Node.js runs JavaScript on one main thread, so CPU-heavy work needs `worker_threads` or separate processes. CPython's standard build has a global interpreter lock that stops threads running Python code simultaneously, so CPU-bound Python typically uses multiple processes. Optional free-threaded builds have been available since Python 3.13. Go and Java run threads across cores by default.

Containers add a common surprise. A runtime that sizes itself from the host's core count may start far more threads than its CPU limit allows, and the container gets throttled, showing latency spikes while average CPU looks moderate. Check that pool sizes reflect the container's limit.
quotes: We doubled the cores and the API didn't get any faster.
It's I/O-bound. Parallelism won't help when every request is waiting on the same database.

nodes.name: Thread
nodes.description: An independent path of execution inside a process, with its own stack but sharing the process's memory with other threads.
nodes.markdown:
A thread is an independent path of execution inside a process. Each thread has its own stack and instruction position, while all threads in a process share the same heap memory and open files. Sharing makes communication between them easy and is also the source of most [concurrency](node:Concurrency) bugs.

The operating system's scheduler decides which threads run and can pause one at nearly any instruction. On a multi-core machine, several run at once, giving [parallelism](node:Parallelism). Even a single line such as `count += 1` is usually several machine steps, so another thread can run between them and cause a [race condition](node:Race%20condition).

| Unit             | Scheduled by     | Memory                | Relative cost |
| ---------------- | ---------------- | --------------------- | ------------- |
| Process          | Operating system | Isolated              | Highest       |
| OS thread        | Operating system | Shared within process | Medium        |
| Virtual thread or goroutine | Language runtime | Shared, small growable stack | Low |

The traditional server model gives each request its own thread. It is easy to reason about, because code runs top to bottom and [blocking I/O](node:Blocking%20IO) only pauses that one thread. Its limit is cost. Each OS thread reserves stack space, and switching between many of them consumes CPU time. A service creating one thread per connection can fail during a traffic spike with an error such as Java's `unable to create native thread`, even though the CPU is barely busy.

Servers therefore reuse a fixed set through a [thread pool](node:Thread%20pool), or use lighter units such as goroutines and Java virtual threads.

Threads in a process share its failures. An uncaught fatal error or memory corruption in one can bring down the entire process. When a service hangs, a thread dump, a snapshot of what each thread is doing, is usually the first diagnostic to take.
quotes: The service stopped responding, but CPU is at 2%.
Take a thread dump. If every thread is parked on the same call, we've found what's holding them up.

nodes.name: Thread pool
nodes.description: A fixed set of reusable threads that take tasks from a queue, bounding how much work a server runs at once.
nodes.markdown:
A [thread](node:Thread) pool is a set of long-lived threads that take tasks from a queue and run them. Reusing threads avoids the cost of creating one per task, and the fixed size caps how much work runs at the same time.

| Step | Who         | What happens                                              |
| ---- | ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Caller      | Submits a task                                            |
| 2    | Pool        | Assigns it to an idle thread, or places it in the queue   |
| 3    | Thread      | Runs the task to completion                               |
| 4    | Thread      | Returns to the pool and takes the next task               |
| 5    | Pool        | Rejects the task if the queue is full                     |

The characteristic failure is pool exhaustion. One slow dependency makes every thread wait on it, new requests pile up in the queue, and the entire service appears hung while CPU sits near idle. Endpoints that do not touch the slow dependency also time out, because they cannot get a thread. Set timeouts on every outbound call, and give risky dependencies their own small pool.

Sizing depends on the work. For CPU-bound tasks, start near the number of cores. For tasks that mostly wait on I/O, a larger pool makes sense, but keep it consistent with downstream limits: 200 threads sharing 20 database connections will queue for connections instead.

Bound the queue. An unbounded queue hides overload until memory runs out, and requests wait so long that clients have already given up. Rejecting early with a 503 [status code](node:Status%20code) is usually better.

A task that submits a subtask to the same pool and waits for it can cause a [deadlock](node:Deadlock) when all threads are doing this. Because threads are reused, thread-local data left by one request, such as a user ID, can leak into the next unless it is cleared.
quotes: Even the health check is timing out, and the CPU is idle.
The thread pool's exhausted. Every thread is stuck on that payment call because it has no timeout.

nodes.name: Event loop
nodes.description: A loop that waits for ready events and runs their callbacks on one thread, letting it serve many connections that mostly wait.
nodes.markdown:
An event loop is a loop that waits for events, such as data arriving on a socket, and runs the code registered for each one. It lets a single [thread](node:Thread) serve thousands of connections, because a connection that is waiting for data costs no thread. Node.js, Python's asyncio, Nginx and Redis are built around this design.

| Step | Who         | What happens                                                  |
| ---- | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Application | Starts an I/O operation and registers what to do on completion |
| 2    | Event loop  | Continues with other ready work                               |
| 3    | OS          | Reports ready sockets through a mechanism such as epoll or kqueue |
| 4    | Event loop  | Queues the matching callback or resumes the paused task       |
| 5    | Event loop  | Runs it until it finishes or yields, then repeats             |

Scheduling is cooperative: nothing interrupts running code. A task keeps the thread until it returns or reaches an `await` in [async-await](node:Async-await) code. The main failure follows from this: one slow operation freezes every other request in the process. A 2-second `JSON.parse` on a large payload, a synchronous file read, an expensive regular expression or [password hashing](node:Password%20hashing) on the main thread means all users wait 2 seconds.

The symptom is latency rising across all endpoints at once, with one CPU core at 100%. Measure event loop lag, the delay between when a callback was due and when it ran.

To keep the loop responsive, avoid [blocking I/O](node:Blocking%20IO) on it. Move CPU-heavy work to a separate thread, a separate process or a [background job](node:Background%20job). Limit request body sizes and split long computations.

"Single-threaded" describes the part that runs your code. Node.js also uses a small internal [thread pool](node:Thread%20pool) for some file, DNS lookup and crypto operations. It has four threads by default, so those operations can queue behind each other.
quotes: Every endpoint spikes whenever someone downloads the big report.
The report builder runs on the event loop and blocks it. Move it off the main thread.

nodes.name: Blocking IO
nodes.description: An input or output call that stops the calling thread until it completes, leaving that thread unable to do anything else.
nodes.markdown:
Blocking I/O is an input or output operation that suspends the calling [thread](node:Thread) until it completes. A call such as `read()` on a socket does not return until data arrives. While it waits, the thread uses almost no CPU, but it cannot do anything else. Network calls, disk access and database queries are the usual examples.

Non-blocking I/O returns control immediately, and the program learns later that the operation has finished.

| Aspect              | Blocking                         | Non-blocking                               |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Code style          | Sequential and easy to read      | [Async-await](node:Async-await), callbacks |
| Waiting costs       | One thread per in-flight call    | A small record per in-flight call          |
| Typical server      | [Thread pool](node:Thread%20pool) | [Event loop](node:Event%20loop)           |
| Main risk           | Running out of threads           | One blocking call stalls everyone          |

Blocking is fine in a threaded server, provided the pool is sized for it and every call has a timeout. Without a timeout, a dependency that stops answering holds its thread indefinitely, and enough of those calls will exhaust the pool.

The damaging case is a blocking call inside an event loop. In Node.js, `fs.readFileSync` stops every request in the process while it runs. In Python, calling `time.sleep()` or the synchronous `requests` library inside an `async def` handler freezes the loop in the same way. The code looks correct and passes tests with one user, then throughput collapses under load because requests are handled one at a time.

To fix it, use the async version of the library, or move the call to a separate thread, for example with `asyncio.to_thread` in Python.

Not all I/O has a non-blocking form on every platform. Regular file reads on Linux generally block even when a descriptor is marked non-blocking, so runtimes such as Node.js hand file operations to helper threads.
quotes: Why does one slow upload stall the whole FastAPI app?
That `async def` handler does blocking I/O with `requests`. Use an async client or run it in a thread.

nodes.name: Async-await
nodes.description: Language syntax for writing non-blocking code in sequential style, pausing a function at each await until its result is ready.
nodes.markdown:
Async-await is language syntax for writing non-blocking code that reads like sequential code. An `async` function can pause at each `await`, handing control back to the scheduler, and resume when the awaited operation completes. JavaScript, Python, C# and Rust all provide it. Usually an [event loop](node:Event%20loop) or similar runtime does the scheduling.

```javascript
async function getOrder(id) {
  const order = await db.findOrder(id); // other tasks run during this wait
  const user = await db.findUser(order.userId);
  return { order, user };
}
```

The compiler or runtime turns such a function into a resumable state machine, so a paused function holds no [thread](node:Thread). This gives [concurrency](node:Concurrency) for I/O-bound work. It does not make CPU-heavy code faster or run it in [parallel](node:Parallelism).

Common mistakes have recognisable symptoms:

| Mistake                         | Symptom                                                 | Fix                                       |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Forgotten `await`               | Code continues early, errors vanish or go unhandled     | Enable a lint rule for floating promises  |
| Awaiting in a loop              | 20 independent calls run one after another              | `Promise.all`, `asyncio.gather`           |
| Unbounded `Promise.all`         | 10,000 calls at once exhaust connections                | Add a concurrency limit                   |
| [Blocking I/O](node:Blocking%20IO) in an async function | Every request stalls                 | Use an async client or a separate thread  |
| Fire-and-forget task            | Work is lost on restart, failures go unseen             | Use a [background job](node:Background%20job) |

A common misconception is that single-threaded async code cannot have a [race condition](node:Race%20condition). It can. Other tasks run at every `await`, so a sequence that reads a balance, awaits something, then writes the balance can interleave with another request doing the same. Keep check-and-update logic free of awaits, or make it atomic in the database.

Async also spreads through a codebase: a function that awaits must generally be async itself, and so must its callers. This is why mixing sync and async libraries takes planning.
quotes: The endpoint makes five API calls and takes five seconds.
You're using async-await one call at a time. They're independent, so run them with `Promise.all`.

nodes.name: Race condition
nodes.description: A bug where the result depends on the timing of overlapping operations, so it appears only under particular interleavings.
nodes.markdown:
A race condition is a bug where the outcome depends on the timing of overlapping operations. The code is correct when steps run one after another and wrong when they interleave. It explains failures such as an oversold last ticket, a coupon redeemed twice, or a counter that ends up lower than the number of requests. These bugs often pass tests and appear only under production load, because [concurrency](node:Concurrency) is what exposes them.

One common form is a lost update:

| Step | Request A      | Request B      | Stored balance |
| ---- | -------------- | -------------- | -------------- |
| 1    | Reads 100      |                | 100            |
| 2    |                | Reads 100      | 100            |
| 3    | Writes 100 - 30 |               | 70             |
| 4    |                | Writes 100 - 50 | 50            |

Both requests succeeded, 80 was withdrawn, and the balance shows only 50 removed. The other common form is check-then-act: two requests both check that a username is free, both see that it is, and both create it. When the gap involves a security check, it is called time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU).

Fixes, in rough order of preference:

| Approach                | Example                                                      |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Atomic operation        | `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 30` |
| Database constraint     | A unique index on `username`, with the conflict handled      |
| Optimistic check        | Update only if a version column is unchanged, else retry     |
| Lock                    | A [mutex](node:Mutex) or a row lock around the critical steps |
| Remove sharing          | Process each account's work through one ordered queue        |

An in-process mutex protects only that process. With several server instances, two requests can hold "the" lock at the same time on different machines, so the rule must be enforced in a shared system such as the database.

Single-threaded runtimes are not immune, because tasks interleave at each `await` in [async-await](node:Async-await) code.
quotes: We sold 102 tickets for a 100-seat venue.
That's a race condition in the availability check. Make the decrement atomic and conditional on remaining seats.

nodes.name: Mutex
nodes.description: A lock that allows only one thread at a time into a section of code, protecting shared data from concurrent access.
nodes.markdown:
A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) is a synchronization primitive that lets only one [thread](node:Thread) at a time run a protected section of code. A thread locks it before touching shared data and unlocks it afterwards. Any other thread attempting to lock it waits. The protected code is called the critical section, and a mutex is a standard fix for a [race condition](node:Race%20condition) on in-memory state.

```go
mu.Lock()
defer mu.Unlock() // released on every return path
balance -= amount
```

Release the lock on every path, using `defer`, `finally` or a scoped guard. If an exception skips the unlock, every later caller waits forever and that code path hangs.

Locks have a performance cost when contended. Since only one thread can hold the mutex, a busy critical section turns parallel work into a single-file line. The symptom is latency that climbs with load while CPU stays low, because threads spend their time waiting.

Practical rules:

| Rule                                   | Reason                                                     |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Keep the critical section short        | Reduces waiting                                            |
| Do not do network or disk calls inside | One slow call stalls every thread needing the lock         |
| Lock consistently                      | One unprotected read or write is still a data race         |
| Acquire several locks in a fixed order | Prevents a [deadlock](node:Deadlock)                       |
| Do not re-lock unless it is reentrant  | Go's `sync.Mutex` deadlocks if the holder locks it again   |

A read-write lock lets many readers in together but gives a writer exclusive access. A reentrant lock, such as Java's `synchronized`, can be taken again by the thread already holding it.

A mutex works only inside one process. It does nothing for two server instances, so rules across instances belong in the database or another shared coordinator. In single-threaded [async-await](node:Async-await) code, an async mutex can protect a sequence that spans an `await`.
quotes: Latency goes up with traffic, but the CPU's only at 20%.
Check the mutex around the cache. It's held during a network call, so every request queues behind it.

nodes.name: Deadlock
nodes.description: A state where tasks wait on each other in a cycle, so none can proceed and the affected work hangs indefinitely.
nodes.markdown:
A deadlock is a state in which two or more tasks each wait for something another holds, so none of them can ever proceed. The typical symptom is a service that stops responding with low CPU and no error in the logs, because nothing has failed.

The simplest case involves two locks:

| Step | Task A           | Task B           |
| ---- | ---------------- | ---------------- |
| 1    | Locks `accounts` |                  |
| 2    |                  | Locks `orders`   |
| 3    | Waits for `orders` |                |
| 4    |                  | Waits for `accounts` |

A deadlock requires four conditions at once, known as the Coffman conditions, and removing any one prevents it:

| Condition        | Meaning                                  | How to break it                          |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Mutual exclusion | A resource has one holder at a time      | Use lock-free or immutable data          |
| Hold and wait    | A task holds one resource, requests more | Acquire everything at once               |
| No preemption    | A resource cannot be taken away          | Use lock timeouts and back off           |
| Circular wait    | Tasks wait in a cycle                    | Always acquire in one global order       |

Consistent ordering is the usual fix. If every code path takes a [mutex](node:Mutex) on the lower account ID first, a transfer from A to B and one from B to A cannot form a cycle.

Deadlocks also occur without explicit locks. A [thread pool](node:Thread%20pool) deadlocks when every [thread](node:Thread) in it waits for subtasks queued in that same pool. A request holding one database connection while waiting for a second can deadlock a small connection pool under load. Calling `.Result` on a task in some C# contexts blocks the thread that the task needs in order to finish.

To diagnose one, take a thread dump and look for tasks waiting on each other. Relational databases detect lock cycles and abort one transaction, so applications should retry that error. Timeouts turn an indefinite hang into a visible failure.
quotes: Transfers hang now and then, always between the same two accounts.
Opposite transfers lock in opposite order, so it's a deadlock. Always lock the lower account ID first.

nodes.name: Background job
nodes.description: Work moved outside the request-response path so it can run later, retry on failure and not keep the user waiting.
nodes.markdown:
A background job is a unit of work that runs outside the [request lifecycle](node:Request%20lifecycle). The handler records that the work must happen, responds to the user and leaves execution to another process. Sending email, generating reports, resizing images and syncing with third parties are typical cases.

The symptom that calls for one is a request doing too much. Signup takes eight seconds because it calls an email provider, and when that provider has an outage, signups start failing even though the account could have been created. Moving the email to a job keeps the endpoint fast and isolates the failure.

Jobs are usually placed on a [job queue](node:Job%20queue) and executed by a [worker](node:Worker). If the client needs the outcome, the API can return `202 Accepted` with a job ID to check, or notify it through a [webhook](node:Webhook) or [Server-Sent Events](node:Server-Sent%20Events).

Job code needs different habits from request code:

| Rule                             | Reason                                                  |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Make it idempotent               | Most queues can deliver a job more than once            |
| Pass IDs, not whole objects      | Data may have changed by the time the job runs          |
| Set a timeout                    | A hung job holds a worker indefinitely                  |
| Keep the payload compatible      | Old jobs may run after new code deploys                 |
| Recheck permissions and state    | The user may have been removed or the order cancelled   |

Timing against the database transaction causes a frequent bug. If you enqueue before the commit, a worker may start immediately, fail to find the row and report "record not found". If you commit and then crash before enqueueing, the job is lost. A transactional outbox solves both: write the job to a table in the same transaction as the data, and have a separate process publish it.
quotes: Checkout is slow because we generate the PDF receipt in the handler.
Make it a background job. Return the order now and email the receipt when it's ready.

nodes.name: Job queue
nodes.description: A durable list of pending background jobs that producers add to and workers take from, with retries and failure handling.
nodes.markdown:
A job queue is a store of pending [background jobs](node:Background%20job). Application code adds jobs, and [workers](node:Worker) take them and run them. The queue separates when work is requested from when it is done, so traffic bursts build up as a backlog instead of overloading the system. Sidekiq, BullMQ and Celery are examples.

A job moves through a lifecycle:

| Step | Who    | What happens                                                   |
| ---- | ------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | App    | Enqueues a job with its type and arguments                     |
| 2    | Worker | Reserves it, making it invisible to others for a lease period  |
| 3    | Worker | Runs the job                                                   |
| 4    | Worker | Acknowledges success, and the queue removes it                 |
| 5    | Queue  | On failure or expired lease, makes it available for retry      |
| 6    | Queue  | After too many attempts, moves it to a dead-letter queue       |

Most queues provide at-least-once delivery. If a worker finishes a job and crashes before acknowledging it, the job runs again. A lease that is shorter than the job's run time causes the same effect while the first worker is still going: two workers process one job and customers receive duplicate emails. Set the lease above the expected duration or extend it while running, and make jobs idempotent.

Retries need delays. Immediate retries against a struggling dependency add load, so use exponential backoff (doubling the wait) with random jitter. Cap the attempts so a poison job, one that can never succeed, does not loop forever. The dead-letter queue holds such jobs for inspection and needs an alert, or failures accumulate unseen.

Monitor the age of the oldest job in addition to queue length. A thousand jobs may be fine for one queue, while a five-minute delay on password-reset emails is an incident. Separate queues by urgency so a large bulk import cannot delay time-sensitive work.
quotes: Password reset emails are arriving forty minutes late.
The marketing send filled the job queue. Put transactional email on its own queue with dedicated workers.

nodes.name: Worker
nodes.description: A long-running process that takes jobs from a queue and executes them, separately from the processes serving web requests.
nodes.markdown:
A worker is a long-running process that repeatedly takes a [background job](node:Background%20job) from a [job queue](node:Job%20queue), runs it and reports the result. Workers usually share the application's codebase but run as separate processes from the web servers, so heavy jobs do not take capacity from user requests and each side can scale independently.

A worker has its own [concurrency](node:Concurrency) setting, the number of jobs it runs at once. The right value depends on the work:

| Job type            | Suggested setup                                     | Reason                             |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| CPU-heavy           | About one job per core                              | More only adds switching           |
| I/O-heavy           | Higher concurrency                                  | Jobs mostly wait                   |
| Memory-heavy        | Low concurrency, dedicated workers                  | Prevents out-of-memory kills       |
| Rate-limited API    | A limit shared across workers                       | Per-process limits add up          |

Adding workers is not always safe. Each one opens connections, so doubling the count can exhaust the database's connection limit and turn a slow backlog into errors for the web application too. Check downstream capacity before scaling, and scale on queue age or depth instead of CPU when jobs mostly wait.

Prefetching causes another surprise. Some systems let a worker reserve several jobs in advance. A worker holding a batch while stuck on one long job leaves the others waiting even though other workers are idle. Lower the prefetch setting for long-running jobs.

Deploys need care because old and new code run at the same time. A new web server can enqueue a job in a format an old worker cannot read, so deploy changes to job payloads in compatible steps. Workers also need [graceful shutdown](node:Graceful%20shutdown): on a stop signal, stop taking new jobs and finish or release current ones.
quotes: We added ten workers to clear the backlog and now the API is throwing connection errors.
Each worker holds its own connections, so we've hit the database limit. Scale back and lower their concurrency.

nodes.name: Cron job
nodes.description: A task that runs automatically on a time-based schedule, such as every night at 2 a.m.
nodes.markdown:
A cron job is a task run automatically on a recurring schedule. The name comes from `cron`, the Unix scheduler, whose five-field expression is now used by many other schedulers. Nightly reports, cleanup of expired data and monthly invoicing are typical uses.

```text
0 2 * * 1-5   run at 02:00, Monday to Friday
```

| Field        | Allowed values |
| ------------ | -------------- |
| Minute       | 0-59           |
| Hour         | 0-23           |
| Day of month | 1-31           |
| Month        | 1-12           |
| Day of week  | 0-7 (0 and 7 are Sunday) |

If both day fields are restricted, standard cron runs when either matches, so `0 0 13 * 5` fires on every 13th and on every Friday.

Most cron problems come from assumptions about how a run behaves:

| Problem           | Symptom                                       | What to do                                   |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| Runs per instance | Scaling to three servers sends three invoices | Use one scheduler, or take a shared lock     |
| Overlapping runs  | A slow job is still going when the next starts | Skip the run if the last is still active    |
| Daylight saving   | A 02:30 job is skipped or runs twice          | Schedule in UTC                              |
| Missed runs       | The host was down at 02:00, so nothing ran    | Process "everything due" instead of "today"  |
| Silent failure    | Backups stopped weeks ago and nobody noticed  | Alert when an expected success does not arrive |

The last row needs a specific control. An alert on failure cannot fire for a job that never started, so have each successful run send a heartbeat and alert when one is missing.

Write the job so that running it twice is harmless, for example by recording which billing period has been processed. Keep the cron entry small: for large tasks, have it enqueue a [background job](node:Background%20job) on a [job queue](node:Job%20queue), which provides retries and visibility.
quotes: Customers got three copies of the monthly invoice.
The cron job runs on every instance, and we scaled to three. Move it to a single scheduler and make it idempotent.

nodes.name: Graceful shutdown
nodes.description: Stopping a server by refusing new work, finishing what is in flight and closing resources before the process exits.
nodes.markdown:
Graceful shutdown is stopping a process in an orderly way: it refuses new work, finishes what is in progress, closes its resources and exits. Without it, each deploy kills in-flight requests, which appears as a burst of 502 errors at every release.

Platforms normally signal a process with `SIGTERM`, wait for a grace period, then force it to stop with `SIGKILL`, which cannot be caught. Kubernetes, for example, waits 30 seconds by default. A server should then:

| Step | Who     | What happens                                                                 |
| ---- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Process | Receives `SIGTERM`                                                           |
| 2    | Process | Fails its readiness check so traffic stops arriving       |
| 3    | Process | Waits briefly, because routing updates are not instant                       |
| 4    | Process | Stops accepting connections and closes idle [keep-alive](node:Keep-alive) ones |
| 5    | Process | Lets in-flight requests finish, up to a deadline                             |
| 6    | Process | Closes database pools and flushes logs and metrics                           |
| 7    | Process | Exits before the grace period ends                                           |

Step 3 is often missed. If the server closes its listener immediately, the load balancer (the component spreading traffic across instances) can still route requests to it for a few seconds, and those requests fail.

A [WebSocket](node:WebSocket) or [Server-Sent Events](node:Server-Sent%20Events) stream never finishes alone, so the server must close it and rely on clients reconnecting with random delay.

A [worker](node:Worker) stops reserving jobs, then finishes the current job or returns it to the [job queue](node:Job%20queue). If a job runs longer than the grace period, it will be killed, so it must be safe to retry.

A common container bug blocks this. If the image starts the app through a shell, as in `CMD node server.js`, the shell may receive `SIGTERM` and not forward it. The app is then killed at the deadline. Use the exec form, `CMD ["node", "server.js"]`.
quotes: We get a spike of 502s on every deploy.
The app has no graceful shutdown. Handle `SIGTERM`, fail readiness, then drain before exiting.

nodes.name: Layered architecture
nodes.description: Organising an application into horizontal layers, such as API, service and data access, where each depends on the one below.
nodes.markdown:
Layered architecture is a way of organising an application into horizontal layers, each with one kind of responsibility. Code in a layer calls the layer beneath it and knows nothing about the layers above. It is the default structure of many web frameworks.

| Layer        | Responsibility                               | Typical contents             |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Presentation | Handle [HTTP](node:HTTP), parse input, format output | Controllers, [DTOs](node:DTO) |
| Application  | Coordinate a use case and its transaction    | Services                     |
| Domain       | Hold business rules                          | Entities, calculations       |
| Data access  | Read and write storage                       | [Repositories](node:Repository%20pattern), [ORM](node:ORM) models |

The purpose is to separate reasons for change. A new response format should affect the presentation layer, and a query optimization should affect data access. The structure also gives a team a shared answer to "where does this code go?"

Layering breaks down in recognisable ways. SQL appears in a controller, so the same rule gets reimplemented in three endpoints with slight differences. Business logic lands in controllers, so a [background job](node:Background%20job) that needs the same rule has to copy it, because it has no HTTP request to pass through. Keeping rules below the presentation layer lets every entry point reuse them.

The opposite failure is ceremony. A service method that only calls a repository method, which only calls the ORM, adds files without adding behaviour. Adding one field then means editing every layer. For a small CRUD service (one that mainly creates, reads, updates and deletes records), fewer layers are reasonable.

A further limitation is the direction of dependencies. In the traditional form, business logic depends on the data layer, so database details can leak upward and the rules are hard to test alone. [Hexagonal architecture](node:Hexagonal%20architecture) inverts that dependency using interfaces and [dependency injection](node:Dependency%20injection).
quotes: Where should the discount calculation go? It's in the controller right now.
Move it down. In our layered architecture, the [worker](node:Worker) and the API should both call the same domain code.

nodes.name: Hexagonal architecture
nodes.description: Structuring an app so business logic sits at the centre and reaches databases, APIs and UIs only through interfaces called ports.
nodes.markdown:
Hexagonal architecture, also called ports and adapters, is a structure that keeps business logic independent of technical details. Alistair Cockburn proposed it. The application sits at the centre and communicates with the outside world only through interfaces called ports. Adapters implement those ports for specific technologies.

| Part            | What it is                                  | Example                            |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Application     | Use cases and business rules                | `PlaceOrder`                       |
| Inbound port    | How the outside calls the application       | `PlaceOrder.execute(command)`      |
| Inbound adapter | Translates an external trigger into a call  | [HTTP](node:HTTP) controller, queue consumer |
| Outbound port   | What the application needs from outside     | `PaymentGateway` interface         |
| Outbound adapter | Implements that need with a technology     | Stripe client, Postgres [repository](node:Repository%20pattern) |

The defining rule is that dependencies point inward. The application defines `PaymentGateway`, and the payment adapter implements it. This differs from traditional [layered architecture](node:Layered%20architecture), where business code usually depends directly on the data layer. Adapters are connected at startup, normally through [dependency injection](node:Dependency%20injection).

The structure addresses a familiar problem: business logic that cannot be tested without a running database and a sandbox payment account, or a vendor's SDK types spread across hundreds of files so that changing vendors becomes a rewrite. With ports, a [unit test](node:Unit%20test) can run a use case with a [test double](node:Test%20double) for each outbound port. The same use case can be triggered by HTTP, a [cron job](node:Cron%20job) or a [worker](node:Worker) by adding an adapter.

The cost is indirection. Each external interaction needs an interface, an adapter and mapping code, which is unnecessary for a thin CRUD application with few rules. A port that mirrors a vendor's API keeps the coupling it was supposed to remove, so define ports in terms of what the application needs. Adapters still need an [integration test](node:Integration%20test), since test doubles cannot show that the real technology behaves as assumed.
quotes: Replacing the payment provider means touching 200 files.
Because the SDK leaked everywhere. With hexagonal architecture, we'd only write a new adapter for the payment port.

nodes.name: Dependency injection
nodes.description: Passing an object the things it depends on from outside, instead of having it create or look them up itself.
quotes: I can't test this service without it sending a real email.
It builds its own mail client. Use dependency injection so the test can pass in a fake.

nodes.name: Repository pattern
nodes.description: Hiding data access behind a collection-like interface so business code asks for domain objects without knowing about queries.
nodes.markdown:
The repository pattern places data access behind an interface that resembles a collection of domain objects. Business code calls methods such as `orders.findById(id)` or `orders.save(order)` and does not need to know how the data is stored. The pattern was described in Martin Fowler's catalogue of enterprise patterns and is a building block of [domain-driven design](node:Domain-driven%20design).

```typescript
interface OrderRepository {
  findById(id: OrderId): Promise<Order | null>;
  findOverdue(asOf: Date): Promise<Order[]>;
  save(order: Order): Promise<void>;
}
```

It addresses query logic scattered across a codebase. When the definition of an "active customer" appears in fifteen handwritten queries, a change to the rule leaves some of them behind, and reports begin to disagree. A named method such as `findActive()` puts the definition in one place. The interface also lets a [unit test](node:Unit%20test) use an in-memory [test double](node:Test%20double), and it serves as an outbound port in [hexagonal architecture](node:Hexagonal%20architecture).

The pattern is often misapplied:

| Misuse                          | Result                                                  | Better approach                       |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Generic `Repository<T>` for all | A thin wrapper repeating the [ORM](node:ORM)            | Methods named for real queries        |
| Returning query builders        | Storage details leak to callers                         | Return domain objects                 |
| Loops calling `findById`        | One query per item, slow lists                          | Add a batch method                    |
| One method per screen           | The interface grows without limit                       | Use separate read queries             |
| Each repository commits alone   | A multi-step operation can half-succeed                 | Manage the transaction at the use case |

Transactions need attention. If `orders.save()` and `inventory.save()` commit separately, a failure between them leaves inconsistent data. Have the application layer open one transaction, sometimes through a unit-of-work object, that both repositories join.

An in-memory fake will not reproduce real constraints, collation or locking, so test the actual repository with an [integration test](node:Integration%20test). For small applications where an ORM already provides a clear interface, adding repositories may only add a layer.
quotes: Finance and support are showing different counts of active customers.
Each has its own query. Put the rule in one repository method and use it in both.

nodes.name: DTO
nodes.description: A simple object that carries data across a boundary, keeping the API's shape separate from internal models.
nodes.markdown:
A DTO (data transfer object) is a simple object that carries data across a boundary, such as between an API and application code. It holds fields and has no business behaviour. Its purpose is to make the shape of data at the boundary explicit and independent from internal models.

Without a DTO, handlers often serialize the database model directly. This causes two well-known security failures:

| Failure            | What happens                                                            | DTO fix                       |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Data exposure      | A new `password_hash` or `internal_notes` column appears in API responses | Response DTO lists allowed fields |
| Mass assignment    | A client adds `"is_admin": true` to a profile update and it gets saved  | Request DTO omits that field  |

Both happen quietly. Nobody edits the endpoint: someone adds a column, and the API starts returning it. An explicit allowlist of fields makes exposure a deliberate decision and supports field-level [authorization](node:Authorization).

```typescript
type CreateUserRequest = { email: string; name: string };
type UserResponse = { id: string; email: string; name: string };
```

Separate DTOs for requests and responses are normally clearer, because their fields differ. A client should not send an `id` or `createdAt`, while a response contains them.

DTOs also protect the public contract. If a response is tied to an [ORM](node:ORM) entity, renaming a column becomes a [breaking change](node:Breaking%20change) for API clients. With a DTO, you change the mapping and leave the API alone.

Validate request DTOs at the edge of the system. Check types, required fields and sizes before the data reaches business code, using a schema library where possible. Remember that a type annotation alone usually has no runtime effect, as with TypeScript types, so incoming JSON still needs validation.

The cost is mapping code and some repetition. For an internal tool with few fields, that can outweigh the benefit, but a public API usually justifies it.
quotes: Why is `password_hash` in the user API response?
The controller returns the ORM entity directly. Add a response DTO that lists only the public fields.

nodes.name: ORM
nodes.description: A library that maps database tables to objects in code and generates SQL for reading and writing them.
nodes.markdown:
An ORM (object-relational mapper) is a library that maps database tables to classes and rows to objects, and generates the SQL to read and write them. Hibernate, Entity Framework, SQLAlchemy and Active Record are common examples. Instead of writing an `INSERT`, you create an object and save it.

An ORM removes repetitive query and mapping code, and its standard query methods use bound parameters, which protects them from [SQL injection](node:SQL%20injection). Many also track changes to loaded objects and write them in one transaction.

The trade-off is that database work becomes less visible. A line that looks like property access can run a query, and this leads to the failures most ORM users eventually meet:

| Problem           | Symptom                                               | What to do                                |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| N+1 queries       | A page of 50 orders runs 51 queries                   | Eager-load the relation or batch it       |
| Over-fetching     | A list loads large text columns it never shows        | Select only needed columns                |
| Lazy load after close | Error when serializing outside the session        | Load data before leaving the transaction  |
| Bulk updates      | Hooks and validations are skipped                     | Know which APIs bypass model logic        |

N+1 usually passes in development with three rows, then becomes a slow endpoint in production. Turn on SQL logging locally, and consider a test that asserts the number of queries for important endpoints.

Use raw SQL when the ORM gets in the way, such as for reports, window functions or bulk changes. Mixing the two is normal. Raw queries must still use bound parameters.

Avoid passing ORM entities through the entire application. Exposing them from an API couples your contract to your table structure, which is what a [DTO](node:DTO) prevents. A [repository](node:Repository%20pattern) can keep ORM details out of business logic.
quotes: This endpoint is fine locally but takes four seconds in production.
Turn on query logging. I'd bet the ORM is lazy-loading the customer for each order.

nodes.name: Domain-driven design
nodes.description: An approach that shapes software around a model of the business, built with domain experts and using their language in code.
nodes.markdown:
Domain-driven design (DDD) is an approach to software that shapes code around a shared model of the business problem. Eric Evans introduced it in his 2003 book of the same name. Developers work with domain experts, such as accountants or logistics planners, so that the concepts in the code match how the business operates.

It targets a recognisable problem. The business says "a policy lapses", the code says `status = 3`, and every requirement has to be translated in someone's head. DDD answers this with a ubiquitous language: an agreed vocabulary used in conversation, documents, class names and method names, such as `policy.lapse()`.

DDD has two levels. The strategic level divides a large domain into parts, each with a [bounded context](node:Bounded%20context) in which terms have one precise meaning. The tactical level gives patterns for modelling inside a context:

| Building block | Meaning                                              | Example                  |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Entity         | Has an identity that persists as data changes        | `Order #42`              |
| Value object   | Defined by its values, usually immutable             | `Money(10, "EUR")`       |
| Aggregate      | A cluster changed as a unit through one root         | `Order` and its lines    |
| Domain event   | A record of something that happened                  | `OrderShipped`           |
| [Repository](node:Repository%20pattern) | Loads and saves aggregates | `OrderRepository` |

Aggregates protect business rules. If an order total must equal the sum of its lines, all changes go through the `Order` root, so no code can update one line and leave the total wrong.

DDD has a real cost and suits complex, long-lived business domains. A simple CRUD application gains little from aggregates and domain services. A common failure is adopting the tactical patterns without talking to domain experts, which adds classes without improving the model. It pairs well with [hexagonal architecture](node:Hexagonal%20architecture), which keeps the model free of infrastructure.
quotes: The code calls it `status 3`, but operations calls it 'on hold pending review'.
Domain-driven design would have us use their term in the code, so we stop translating.

nodes.name: Bounded context
nodes.description: A boundary within which a domain model and its terms have one consistent meaning, even if other areas use the words differently.
nodes.markdown:
A bounded context is an explicit boundary inside which a model and its vocabulary have one consistent meaning. The term comes from [domain-driven design](node:Domain-driven%20design). It accepts that a large business does not have one universal model, because the same word means different things to different departments.

| Context  | What "customer" means               | Fields it cares about           |
| -------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Sales    | A lead or account being pursued     | Stage, owner, expected value    |
| Billing  | The party that pays invoices        | Tax ID, payment method, balance |
| Shipping | A recipient at an address           | Address, delivery instructions  |
| Support  | A person with open tickets          | Plan, ticket history            |

Without boundaries, these meanings merge into a single model. The symptom is a `User` or `Customer` class with a hundred fields and many nullable columns, which every team edits and nobody fully understands. A billing change breaks shipping, and developers argue over what "active" means because each team is correct about its own area.

Inside each bounded context, the model contains only what that context needs. Billing has its own `Customer`, shipping has its own `Recipient`, and they relate through a shared identifier. Some duplication is intended, since it allows each model to change independently.

Contexts communicate through explicit contracts, such as an API, a [webhook](node:Webhook) or published events. When one integrates with a messy or external model, it can use an anti-corruption layer, code that translates the foreign model at the edge so its concepts do not leak inward. A [DTO](node:DTO) often carries the data across this boundary.

A bounded context is a design boundary and does not have to be a separate service. It can be a module inside one deployable application, which is often a sensible starting point. Enforce it by not reaching into another context's tables or internal classes.
quotes: Should we add `shipping_notes` to the main `Customer` model?
No, that belongs to the shipping bounded context. Keep it on `Recipient` and link by customer ID.

nodes.name: Unit test
nodes.description: A fast, isolated test of one small piece of behaviour, run without a network, real database or other external system.
nodes.markdown:
A unit test is an automated test that checks a small piece of behaviour in isolation. It runs in memory, with no network or real database, so a suite of thousands can finish in seconds and give feedback while you code. Teams disagree on the size of a "unit": it may be one function, one class or a small group of collaborating objects.

```python
def test_discount_is_capped_at_fifty_percent():
    order = Order(subtotal=Money(100))        # arrange
    order.apply_discount(percent=80)          # act
    assert order.total == Money(50)           # assert
```

Unit tests suit logic with many cases: pricing, validation, parsing, date handling and state transitions. Boundary values such as zero, empty input, the maximum and the day of a leap year are cheap to cover here and expensive to cover any other way.

Good unit tests share a few properties:

| Property      | What it means                                      |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Fast          | Milliseconds each, so people run them constantly   |
| Deterministic | Same result every run, with clock and randomness controlled |
| Isolated      | No dependence on other tests or their order        |
| Behavioural   | Asserts outcomes, not internal steps               |
| Readable      | The name states the rule being protected           |

The common failure is coupling tests to implementation. A test asserting that a private helper was called twice breaks when you refactor, even though the behaviour is unchanged. After enough false alarms, people stop trusting the suite and refactoring slows down. Overuse of a mocking [test double](node:Test%20double) is the usual cause. Prefer checking return values and resulting state, and use doubles mainly for slow or external dependencies.

Unit tests cannot show that components work together. A query can be mocked successfully and still contain invalid SQL, which is what an [integration test](node:Integration%20test) is for. The [test pyramid](node:Test%20pyramid) describes how to balance these levels. Code that is difficult to unit test often has hard-wired dependencies, which [dependency injection](node:Dependency%20injection) can loosen.
quotes: I renamed one private method and 40 unit tests failed.
They're asserting on internals. Rewrite them to check the output, so a refactor doesn't break them.

nodes.name: Integration test
nodes.description: A test that runs your code against real collaborators, such as a database, to check that the parts work together.
nodes.markdown:
An integration test checks that your code works correctly with a real collaborator, such as a database, message broker or another module. A [unit test](node:Unit%20test) replaces those dependencies, so it cannot catch a mistaken assumption about how they behave. Integration tests catch failures that appear at the join.

The familiar symptom is a green test suite followed by a production failure. The mocked [repository](node:Repository%20pattern) returned a row, but the real query had a typo. The code inserted a duplicate that the real unique constraint rejected. A timestamp lost precision, a migration was missing, or JSON serialized differently from what the test assumed.

Good targets include:

| Target                                     | What it can catch                                  |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Repository and [ORM](node:ORM) queries | Invalid SQL, constraints, N+1, collation |
| [HTTP](node:HTTP) route through [middleware](node:Middleware) | Routing, [authentication](node:Authentication), [status codes](node:Status%20code) |
| [Job queue](node:Job%20queue) flows        | Serialization, retries, acknowledgement            |
| Transaction behaviour                      | Rollbacks and isolation between operations         |
| Client for an external API                 | Parsing, timeouts and error mapping, using a local stub server |

Use the same database engine as production. Running tests on SQLite while production uses PostgreSQL hides differences in types, locking and SQL dialect. Tools such as Testcontainers start a real database in a container, disposable per test run.

Isolation is the main practical challenge. Tests sharing a database can interfere and produce a [flaky test](node:Flaky%20test) that only fails when run in a certain order or in parallel. Common solutions include wrapping each test in a transaction that rolls back, giving each test process its own schema, or generating unique data per test.

Integration tests are slower than unit tests, so keep them focused on the boundary and leave detailed business-rule permutations to faster tests. For a dependency owned by another team, a [contract test](node:Contract%20test) is often more practical than running their full system.
quotes: All the tests pass, but the deploy fails on a unique constraint.
The repository is mocked everywhere. Add an integration test against a real Postgres container.

nodes.name: Contract test
nodes.description: A test verifying that an API provider and its consumer agree on request and response format, without running both together.
nodes.markdown:
A contract test verifies that two services agree on the format of their communication, without deploying them together. The contract records the requests a consumer sends and the responses it depends on. Each side then tests against that record independently.

It addresses a specific gap. Team A's tests mock Team B's API and pass. Team B's tests pass too. Then B renames a field, both pipelines stay green, and the failure appears only after deployment. Each side was testing against its own assumption. A contract test turns that mismatch into a failing build before the [breaking change](node:Breaking%20change) ships.

In consumer-driven contract testing, the flow is as follows:

| Step | Who      | What happens                                                           |
| ---- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Consumer | Writes a test declaring the request it sends and the fields it needs   |
| 2    | Tool     | Runs that test against a mock and generates a contract file            |
| 3    | Consumer | Publishes the contract to a shared location                            |
| 4    | Provider | Replays the contract against its real code in CI, the automated build  |
| 5    | Both     | Check compatibility before deploying                                   |

Pact is a widely used tool for this approach. When every consumer publishes a contract, a provider can see which fields are unused.

An alternative is schema-based testing, where both sides are checked against a shared [OpenAPI](node:OpenAPI) document or [Protocol Buffers](node:Protocol%20Buffers) definition. This is simpler to adopt and suits public APIs with unknown consumers, but it shows only that a schema is compatible, and it says nothing about which fields clients rely on.

Contract tests check structure and agreed interactions. They do not verify business logic, so a response with the correct shape and a wrong price still passes. Keep those checks in the provider's [unit tests](node:Unit%20test) and [integration tests](node:Integration%20test).
quotes: Their deploy broke our checkout again, and both CI pipelines were green.
We're mocking their API from memory. Add a contract test so their build fails if they drop a field we use.

nodes.name: Test double
nodes.description: A stand-in for a real dependency during a test. Dummies, stubs, spies, mocks and fakes are the main kinds.
nodes.markdown:
A test double is an object that replaces a real dependency during a test, in the way a stunt double replaces an actor. Gerard Meszaros coined the term in his book _xUnit Test Patterns_. Doubles let a [unit test](node:Unit%20test) avoid sending real email, charging a real card or waiting on a network, and they make hard-to-trigger cases, such as a timeout, easy to simulate.

"Mock" is commonly used for all of them, but there are five distinct kinds:

| Kind  | What it does                                  | Example                                  |
| ----- | --------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Dummy | Fills a parameter and is never used           | A placeholder logger                     |
| Stub  | Returns canned answers                        | `getRate()` always returns `1.2`         |
| Spy   | Records how it was called                     | Captures emails "sent" for later checks  |
| Mock  | Is preprogrammed with expected calls and verifies them | Fails unless `charge(100)` is called once |
| Fake  | Has a working but simplified implementation   | An in-memory [repository](node:Repository%20pattern) |

Choosing the right kind affects how brittle a suite becomes. Stubs and fakes support checking outcomes. Mocks verify interactions, which fits cases where the call itself is the behaviour, such as "the payment was charged exactly once". Using mocks for every collaborator ties tests to implementation, so a harmless refactor turns the suite red.

The larger risk is drift. A double encodes your belief about how the dependency behaves, and it keeps passing after the real one changes. The stub returns `{ "amount": 100 }` while the real API now returns a string, so tests stay green and production fails. An [integration test](node:Integration%20test) or [contract test](node:Contract%20test) keeps those beliefs honest.

Double what you own, by wrapping a third-party SDK in a small interface of your own and replacing that interface. Inject doubles through [dependency injection](node:Dependency%20injection) instead of patching globals, which can leak between tests and cause a [flaky test](node:Flaky%20test).
quotes: The payment test passes, but real charges are failing.
Our test double still returns the old response format. Add a contract test against the provider.

nodes.name: Test pyramid
nodes.description: A model for balancing a test suite, with many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and a small number of end-to-end tests.
nodes.markdown:
The test pyramid is a model for deciding how many tests to write at each level. Mike Cohn popularised it. Its shape reflects cost: the base holds many fast, cheap tests, and each level above holds fewer, slower and more realistic ones.

| Level                                     | Quantity | Speed    | Confidence given             | Failure points to     |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------- | -------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------- |
| End-to-end                                | Few      | Slow     | The full system works        | Anywhere              |
| [Integration](node:Integration%20test)    | Some     | Medium   | Components work together     | A specific boundary   |
| [Unit](node:Unit%20test)                  | Many     | Fast     | Logic is correct             | A small area of code  |

An end-to-end test drives the deployed system as a user or client would. It catches wiring problems nothing else can, but it is slow, can fail for unrelated reasons, and a failure reveals little about the cause.

The usual rule is to test each behaviour at the lowest level that can catch its bug. Cover all discount permutations in unit tests. Use one integration test to show that the discount persists, and one end-to-end test to show that checkout works.

The recognisable anti-pattern is the inverted pyramid, or "ice cream cone". Most coverage sits in browser or end-to-end tests. CI, the automated build, takes an hour, a [flaky test](node:Flaky%20test) fails most runs, and developers rerun the pipeline until it passes or stop reading the results. When a test fails at the top and no lower test failed with it, consider adding the missing lower-level test.

The pyramid is a guideline and not a fixed ratio. A thin API over a database has little isolated logic, so integration tests may provide most of the value. That view is reflected in alternatives such as the "testing trophy". A [contract test](node:Contract%20test) can replace many slow cross-service end-to-end tests.
quotes: CI takes 70 minutes, and most of that is Selenium.
Our test pyramid is upside down. Keep a few critical journeys and push the rest down to API and unit tests.

nodes.name: Flaky test
nodes.description: A test that passes and fails on the same code with no change, usually because of timing, shared state or environment.
nodes.markdown:
A flaky test is a test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails on identical code. It often appears as a test that passes alone and fails in CI, the automated build, or a pipeline that goes green when someone presses "re-run". The damage spreads beyond the single test: once people expect random failures, they start ignoring real ones.

Most flakiness has a small set of causes:

| Cause            | Example                                                | Fix                                         |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------- |
| Timing           | `sleep(1)` before checking a [background job](node:Background%20job) | Poll for the condition with a timeout |
| Shared state     | Tests reuse one database row or global variable        | Isolate data per test                       |
| Test order       | One test depends on another's leftovers                | Run in random order to expose it            |
| Clock            | Fails at midnight, month-end or in another timezone    | Inject a fixed clock                        |
| Unordered results | Asserting on a query with no `ORDER BY`               | Sort, or compare as a set                   |
| Network          | Calls a real third-party sandbox                       | Use a [test double](node:Test%20double) or stub server |
| Code bug         | A [race condition](node:Race%20condition) in the code  | Fix the production bug                      |

The last row is why flakiness should not be dismissed. A test failing once in fifty runs may be correctly detecting a race that also hits customers.

To reproduce one, run it in a loop, run the suite with the same order seed, and limit CPU to mimic CI.

Automatic retries keep a pipeline moving, but they also hide the problem. If you use them, record every test that passed only on retry. Quarantine a known flaky test by moving it out of the blocking suite, assign an owner and set a deadline.

[Integration tests](node:Integration%20test) and end-to-end tests are more prone to this, which is one reason the [test pyramid](node:Test%20pyramid) keeps them fewer.
quotes: Just re-run it, that test always fails on Fridays.
That's a flaky test with a date bug. Inject the clock and fix it instead of re-running.
